content: Isoniazid injection is an FDA-approved antibacterial agent used for the treatment of all forms of tuberculosis caused by susceptible organisms. It is also indicated for individuals with HIV infection, close contacts of newly diagnosed infectious tuberculosis cases, and recent tuberculin skin test converters. Preventive therapy is recommended for specific high-risk groups, including those with HIV, individuals with abnormal chest radiographs suggestive of healed tuberculosis, and intravenous drug users. The drug carries a Black Box Warning due to the risk of severe and potentially fatal hepatitis. Common adverse reactions include peripheral neuropathy, nausea, vomiting, elevated liver enzymes, and fatigue. Peripheral neuropathy is dose-related and more common in malnourished individuals or those predisposed to neuropathy, such as alcoholics and diabetics. For adults, isoniazid is administered at 5 mg/kg daily (up to 300 mg) or 15 mg/kg (up to 900 mg) two to three times weekly. For children, the dose is 10-15 mg/kg daily (up to 300 mg) or 20-40 mg/kg (up to 900 mg) two to three times weekly. Therapy for active tuberculosis must include multiple drugs to prevent resistance. Single-drug therapy is inadequate for active disease. Isoniazid is contraindicated in patients with severe hypersensitivity reactions, drug-induced hepatitis, or acute liver disease. It should be used cautiously in individuals with chronic liver disease, alcohol use, or conditions predisposing to neuropathy. Monitoring of liver function tests is essential, especially in patients over 35 years of age or those with risk factors for hepatotoxicity. The drug should not be administered with food, as its bioavailability is reduced. Foods containing tyramine or histamine should be avoided due to potential interactions. Isoniazid may interact with other medications, such as acetaminophen, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and theophylline, necessitating close monitoring and dosage adjustments. In pregnancy, isoniazid is classified as Category C. It crosses the placenta and is present in breast milk, but the levels are not sufficient for prophylaxis in nursing infants. Preventive therapy is generally deferred until after delivery unless the benefits outweigh the risks. Overdose of isoniazid can result in symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, dizziness, seizures, and metabolic acidosis. Severe cases may lead to respiratory distress, coma, and intractable seizures. Prompt treatment is critical to manage these complications. DOT involves a healthcare provider observing the patient ingesting the medication to improve adherence and treatment outcomes.
